title: Pressure Due to the Weight of Fluid

changes.local: What do you suppose is the total pressure at a depth of 10.3 m in a swimming pool? Does the atmospheric pressure on the water’s surface affect the pressure below? The answer is yes. This seems only logical, since both the water’s weight and the atmosphere’s weight must be supported. So the total pressure at a depth of 10.3 m is 2 atm—half from the water above and half from the air above.

changes.local: This value is the pressure due to the weight of a fluid. The equation has general validity beyond the special conditions under which it is derived here. Even if the container were not there, the surrounding fluid would still exert this pressure, keeping the fluid static. Thus the equation [MATH] represents the pressure due to the weight of any fluid of average density [MATH] at any depth [MATH] below its surface. For liquids, which are nearly incompressible, this equation holds to great depths.

changes.local_html: This value is the pressure due to the weight of a fluid. The equation has general validity beyond the special conditions under which it is derived here. Even if the container were not there, the surrounding fluid would still exert this pressure, keeping the fluid static. Thus the equation P=ρgh represents the pressure due to the weight of any fluid of average density ρ at any depth h below its surface. For liquids, which are nearly incompressible, this equation holds to great depths.

Thus the equation P=hρg represents the pressure due to the weight of any fluid of average density ρ at any depth h below its surface. For gases, which are quite compressible, one can apply this equation as long as the density changes are small over the depth considered. [reference] illustrates this situation.
